hints: Start with solubility, since Q dissolves easily in water this already rules out two of the choices.
Think about what concentrated sulfuric acid does to a solid chloride versus a solid bromide, only one gives clean steamy white fumes.
Use the silver nitrate result to confirm the halide, recall which silver halide is white and dissolves in dilute ammonia.
walkthrough:
**Use solubility to narrow down Q**

Q is described as a white crystalline solid which dissolves easily in water. That is a big clue.

Silver chloride, $\text{AgCl}$, and lead(II) bromide, $\text{PbBr}_2$, are both insoluble in water. So they cannot be Q. This leaves a soluble sodium halide, either $\text{NaBr}$ or $\text{NaCl}$.

**Interpret the reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid**

Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ displaces the hydrogen halide from a solid halide. For a chloride:
$$\text{NaCl(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(l)} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4\text{(s) + HCl(g)}$$ 
$\text{HCl}$ is seen as steamy white fumes. For a bromide, $\text{HBr}$ is first formed but is then oxidised to brown $\text{Br}_2$ fumes plus $\text{SO}_2$. Since only white fumes are seen, Q must contain chloride.

**Confirm with the silver nitrate and ammonia tests**

Passing $\text{HCl}$ gas into water gives $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, which give a white precipitate with silver nitrate:
$$\text{Ag}^+\text{(aq) + Cl}^-\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{AgCl(s)}$$ 
$\text{AgCl}$ is white and dissolves in dilute ammonia to give a colourless solution:
$$\text{AgCl(s) + 2NH}_3\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{[Ag(NH}_3\text{)}_2\text{]}^+\text{(aq) + Cl}^-\text{(aq)}$$ 
This matches exactly. So Q is sodium chloride.

options.A: AgCl is a white solid but it is insoluble in water, so it does not fit 'dissolves easily in water'. It also would not release HCl fumes with concentrated sulfuric acid in this way.
options.B: NaBr is soluble, but bromide with concentrated H2SO4 gives HBr which is oxidised to brown Br2 fumes, not clean white fumes. Its silver test also gives a cream precipitate of AgBr which needs concentrated ammonia to dissolve, not dilute ammonia.
options.C: NaCl is white, crystalline and very soluble. With concentrated H2SO4 it gives steamy white HCl fumes, which reform Cl- in water to give white AgCl precipitate, soluble in dilute ammonia. All three observations fit perfectly.
options.D: PbBr2 is sparingly soluble in water, so it fails the 'dissolves easily' condition. As a bromide it would also give brown bromine fumes and a cream AgBr precipitate, not the white precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia.
